prompt: What separates "agentic" coding tools (Claude Code, Cursor's agent mode, Codex) from classic autocomplete like early GitHub Copilot?
options: They take on whole tasks — reading the codebase, editing multiple files, running tests, and iterating — rather than suggesting the next few lines
They write comments instead of code
explanation: Autocomplete predicts your next lines as you type. Agentic tools operate at task level: 'add auth to this app' triggers codebase exploration, multi-file edits, test runs, and self-correction. This shift from assistant-as-typist to assistant-as-junior-engineer defined the 2025 coding-tools wave.
nuance: The practical skill shifts too: from writing code to specifying tasks well and reviewing AI-written diffs critically.
source_title: The AI Daily Brief (podcast) — agentic coding coverage

prompt: You want an AI system that checks inventory via API, drafts reorder emails, and files tickets — multiple steps and tools. What category of solution is this?
options: An agent — an LLM orchestrated in a loop with tool access (built directly on APIs or with a framework)
explanation: Multi-step workflows with tool calls are agent territory: the model decides which tool to call, interprets results, and chains steps. You can build this with raw API tool-calling or frameworks — the architecture (LLM + tools + loop) is the defining feature.
nuance: Anthropic's 'Building effective agents' guidance: prefer simple, composable patterns (chains, routers) and add full autonomy only when the task truly needs it — reliability drops with every added step.

options: An AI-native code editor (a VS Code fork) with deep model integration for editing, chat, and agentic tasks
explanation: Cursor forked VS Code and rebuilt the experience around AI: inline edits, codebase-aware chat, and agent modes. It became one of the fastest-growing dev tools ever and the poster child for 'AI-native' product design versus AI-features-bolted-on.
nuance: Its rise is a favorite product case study: distribution and UX around models, not owning a model, drove its growth.
source_title: Lenny's Podcast — AI product case studies

prompt: Midjourney, DALL·E, and Stable Diffusion are all…
explanation: All three generate images from text prompts. Their positioning differs: Midjourney for aesthetic quality via a polished service, DALL·E integrated into ChatGPT, and Stable Diffusion as the open-weights option you can run and fine-tune yourself.
nuance: The same trichotomy — polished closed service vs. ecosystem integration vs. open weights — repeats across almost every AI media category.

options: An open-source speech-to-text (transcription) model that became the default building block for audio transcription
explanation: Whisper transcribes audio to text across many languages, and OpenAI released it open-source — which made high-quality transcription essentially free infrastructure. Podcast search tools, meeting-notes apps, and video subtitling widely build on it or its derivatives.
nuance: It's a good example of a lab open-sourcing a 'commodity layer' while keeping frontier models closed.

explanation: ElevenLabs leads in text-to-speech quality and voice cloning — powering audiobook narration, dubbing, agents that talk, and podcast tooling. Voice became one of the fastest-maturing AI modalities in 2024–2025.
nuance: Voice cloning is also a consent and deepfake flashpoint — reputable providers require voice-owner verification, and regulation is tightening.
source_title: The AI Daily Brief (podcast) — voice AI coverage

prompt: What does "vibe coding" (a term popularized by Andrej Karpathy in early 2025) refer to?
options: Building software by conversing with an AI — accepting its code largely without reading it, steering by results and feel
explanation: Karpathy coined 'vibe coding' for the emerging practice of prompting your way to working software — describing what you want, letting the AI write everything, and iterating on outcomes rather than reading diffs. It captured how radically coding tools had changed and enabled a wave of non-engineer builders.
nuance: The serious debate it sparked: fine for prototypes and personal tools, dangerous for production systems where unreviewed code means unreviewed security and correctness.

prompt: What is Google's NotebookLM known for?
options: Source-grounded research: you upload your documents and it answers, summarizes, and can even generate a podcast-style audio discussion from them
explanation: NotebookLM answers questions grounded strictly in the sources you upload (reducing hallucination) and famously generates 'Audio Overviews' — two AI hosts discussing your documents. That feature went viral in late 2024 and made source-grounded AI mainstream.
nuance: It's a useful design reference for AI Quizzer itself: grounding in user-chosen sources plus a novel format is a product, not just a feature.

prompt: Your team is building a customer-support bot on your help docs. What's the recommended starting architecture?
options: Fine-tune a model on transcripts of past support chats
Prompting + RAG over the help docs with a strong off-the-shelf model — iterate there before considering fine-tuning
Train a custom model from scratch
Buy GPUs and self-host an open model first
explanation: The standard playbook: start with the simplest approach (good prompt + retrieval over your docs + capable API model), measure with evals, and only add complexity like fine-tuning if you hit a wall. Most support bots never need more than well-executed RAG.
nuance: Andrew Ng's recurring advice: teams overestimate how often they need fine-tuning and underestimate how far prompting and retrieval go.

prompt: In a RAG system, what role does a vector database (Pinecone, pgvector, Chroma, etc.) play?
options: It stores document embeddings and finds the most semantically similar chunks for a query, fast, even across millions of documents
explanation: Vector databases index embeddings for fast nearest-neighbor search: your query gets embedded, the DB returns the closest document chunks, and those chunks go into the LLM's context. They're the retrieval backbone of most RAG deployments.
nuance: For modest scale you often don't need a dedicated one — pgvector inside Postgres or even an in-memory index covers many products, and simplicity wins.

prompt: What's the core tradeoff of building on an agent/orchestration framework (LangChain, LlamaIndex, etc.) versus calling model APIs directly?
options: Frameworks give speed-to-start and prebuilt integrations, but add abstraction layers that can obscure prompts and complicate debugging; direct API code is more transparent and controllable
Direct APIs can't do tool calling
Frameworks are required for production deployments
explanation: Frameworks bundle patterns (retrieval, memory, tool routing) and save boilerplate. The cost is indirection: when output quality degrades, you may be debugging through layers that rewrite your prompts. Many experienced teams prototype with frameworks, then rebuild critical paths on direct API calls.
nuance: Anthropic's agent guidance explicitly recommends starting with direct API calls and only adopting frameworks once you understand the underlying pattern you need.

prompt: Suno and Udio are AI tools for generating…
explanation: Both generate complete songs — vocals, instruments, structure — from text descriptions. They pushed AI music from novelty to genuinely listenable, and landed at the center of the industry's biggest copyright fights, with major-label lawsuits filed in 2024.
nuance: The training-data copyright question they raise (can you train on copyrighted recordings?) is the same one running through text and image AI litigation.
source_title: The AI Daily Brief (podcast) — AI music coverage

options: An AI answer engine — conversational search that answers questions directly with cited web sources
explanation: Perplexity combines web search with LLM synthesis: you ask a question, it searches, reads, and answers with inline citations. It became the reference example of AI-era search challenging the ten-blue-links model.
nuance: Its rise pressured Google to ship AI Overviews and set off ongoing fights with publishers over content use — the business-model tension of AI search in miniature.

prompt: An internal knowledge chatbot is giving wrong answers. Investigation shows the right documents often aren't in the context at answer time. Where should you focus?
options: Fix retrieval — chunking, embeddings, query handling, and search quality — because no model can answer from documents it never sees
explanation: This is the most common RAG failure and the most common misdiagnosis — teams swap models when the problem is upstream. If retrieval doesn't surface the right chunk, the model either hallucinates or refuses. Debug the pipeline stage that's actually failing.
nuance: A practical trick: log retrieved chunks alongside answers and grade retrieval separately from generation in your evals — two different failure modes, two different fixes.

prompt: True or false: AI coding tools are only useful for professional software engineers.
explanation: False. A defining 2025 shift was non-engineers — PMs, designers, marketers, founders — shipping working tools via agentic coding and app-builder products (Replit, Lovable, v0, Claude Code). 'Ability to code' stopped being the gate; 'ability to specify and evaluate' became the skill.
nuance: Lenny's Newsletter has repeatedly covered PMs prototyping features themselves as a rising expectation in product roles — interviews increasingly assume it.
source_title: Lenny's Newsletter — AI prototyping for PMs
